proposals.name: Deadpan mundane register against an implied extreme situation
proposals.instruction: Score how flatly ordinary the speech is relative to the situation it implies. 10 = completely unexcited, everyday phrasing that treats an evidently strange or dire circumstance as routine business ('and now we wait', 'no idea, let's just take the stairs'); the comedy comes entirely from the mismatch between the calm diction and the implied scene. 5 = normal conversational tone with some comic heightening. 0 = the line is written in obviously comic diction: exclamation, mock-grandeur, whimsy words, or a tone that itself performs 'this is funny'. Judge tone only, not subject matter.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high half is dominated by tonal flatness: R16 ('and now we wait'), R34 ('no idea, let's just take the stairs'), R45 ('try not to overthink it'), R13. The dense-low half raises its voice: R26 ('just my luck! chandelier season...'), R42 ('watch out! if that one escapes...'). A scorecard built from explicit joke-quality items would find nothing to credit in R16 or R13, which is exactly where card_pct collapses (0.132, 0.100) while dense_pct stays high.

proposals.name: Joke is inert as standalone text; needs the drawing to complete
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the joke is withheld from the text and left to an unseen picture. 10 = read alone, the line is an unremarkable sentence with no discernible gag; it can only become funny once a drawing supplies the other half. 5 = partially self-explaining. 0 = a fully freestanding gag: the text alone states a complete joke, and an image would add nothing. Do not reward or penalize whether you personally find it funny; score only the degree of dependence on unseen material.
proposals.rationale: R13 ('did we forget anything') and R49 ('did i miss anything') are nearly contentless as text yet dense_pct 0.868 / 0.907 with card_pct 0.100 / 0.081 — a criterion bank scoring text-visible joke content must floor them. The reverse pole is R33 and R59, complete stand-alone jokes with card_pct 0.797 / 0.896 and the two lowest dense values in the slice (0.059, 0.004). This single axis may account for more of the disagreement than any other.

proposals.name: Payload is not a pun on a depicted object's name
proposals.instruction: Score whether the line's comic payload rests on a homophone or double meaning of a physically depicted object. 10 = no such pun anywhere; the line would survive intact if the object were renamed. 4 = a pun is present but is decoration on an independent idea. 0 = the entire caption exists to deliver one word that means both a scene object and something else ('circus breaker', 'fixture', 'downsizing', 'liquidations', 'best in show'). Score the mechanism, not the cleverness of the pun.
proposals.rationale: R40 ('circus breaker'), R29 ('fixture'), R53 ('downsizing'), R20 ('liquidations'), R55 ('best in show') all sit at card_pct 0.855-0.961 with dense_pct 0.110-0.186. Object-name puns are maximally legible to any explicit criterion ('uses wordplay', 'is clever with language') and are precisely what the dense model appears to discount as a stale move.

proposals.name: Not carried by a dated topical or political name-drop
proposals.instruction: Score independence from news-cycle material. 10 = contains no proper noun, policy, or headline of the moment, and would read identically in ten years. 5 = topical reference present but the joke works without recognizing it. 0 = the punch IS the reference: remove the named figure, policy, dollar amount, or slogan and nothing remains. Judge only whether the topicality is load-bearing.
proposals.rationale: R43 ('marjorie taylor greene'), R52 ('if trump wins again'), R03 ('trump lure'), R28 ('full 1200 stimulus'), R42 ('herd immunity') cluster at card_pct 0.826-0.994 against dense_pct 0.070-0.213. Explicit criteria reward topical relevance and recognizability; the dense model seems to treat borrowed news salience as substituting for invention. Note R04 shows a topical touch can co-occur with high dense_pct when it is not the whole payload — hence 'load-bearing' is the test.

proposals.name: Enters mid-conversation and implies an unheard prior turn
proposals.instruction: Score whether the line is the second (or later) beat of an exchange rather than an opening statement. 10 = it plainly answers or continues something never shown — it begins with 'and', 'no,', 'that's because', or supplies an answer whose question the reader must reconstruct. 5 = addresses someone but starts the exchange. 0 = a self-contained opening pronouncement with no implied interlocutor turn.
proposals.rationale: R18 ('and in exchange, i'll switch from the bass to the viola'), R02 ('about three years. how long have you been here'), R30 ('no, i can't help you get out of it like always...'), R56 ('that's because i am talking in a tin can') are dense_pct 0.719-0.958 with card_pct 0.032-0.219. A criterion bank reading each caption as a complete utterance has no way to credit the implied off-page turn, which is where much of these captions' work is done.

proposals.name: Presupposes an ongoing relationship with accumulated history
proposals.instruction: Score how much prior shared life between speaker and addressee the line presupposes. 10 = unmistakable long-running dynamic: repeated grievances, standing habits, words like 'like always', 'again', 'nobody likes to', a routine both parties already know. 5 = acquaintances with mild familiarity. 0 = strangers, a generic announcement, or an address to no one in particular.
proposals.rationale: R30 ('like always'), R17 ('we're just having game night. what about you'), R27 ('this is why nobody likes to play with you'), R22 ('i suppose this is a good time to let you know...') run dense_pct 0.753-0.974 at card_pct 0.016-0.257. Implied relational history is not a property of the sentence's joke structure, so an explicit bank scoring cleverness, specificity, or wordplay will miss it entirely.

proposals.name: Quietly reassigns power, blame, or who the subject is
proposals.instruction: Score whether the line performs a reversal of standing between the parties or between speaker and their own situation. 10 = the sentence relocates authority, victimhood, or agency in a way the reader must recompute ('you now report directly to me'; 'at least i know i'm a puppet'). 5 = mild status friction. 0 = the expected character says the expected thing from the expected position.
proposals.rationale: R35, R58 ('do you have any idea who you're talking to'), R01 ('at least i know i'm a puppet'), R46 ('can i get a discount? this fish is dead') carry dense_pct 0.820-0.956 against card_pct 0.004-0.264. R17's card_pct of 0.004 with dense_pct 0.913 is the extreme case: nothing in the text is 'clever' by any explicit measure, and the whole effect is a status inversion the reader completes.

proposals.name: No comic signposting or announcement of the punchline
proposals.instruction: Score the absence of self-flagging. 10 = the line never signals that a joke is arriving: no 'wow,', 'watch out!', 'ladies and gentlemen', 'for my next trick', 'just my luck!', no exclamation used as a laugh cue. 5 = one mild interjection. 0 = the caption opens by framing its own gag, or performs a stage-patter register whose only job is to cue the audience.
proposals.rationale: R33 ('for my next trick'), R44 ('ladies and gentlemen'), R54 ('watch me pull out'), R26 ('just my luck!'), R07 ('wow, you student loan people...') hold card_pct 0.730-0.958 with dense_pct 0.038-0.166. Announcement phrasing reads to an explicit judge as confident construction and clear setup-payoff; it appears to read to the dense model as amateur telegraphing.

proposals.name: Adds information rather than narrating what is already drawn
proposals.instruction: Score how much new, non-visible information the line introduces. 10 = every content word points off-page: motive, history, an offstage party, a rule of the world. 5 = mixed. 0 = the caption inventories the picture back to the viewer — naming the depicted object, its size, seat numbers, who is standing where — so that a reader with the image learns nothing.
proposals.rationale: R33 (barefoot guy in 13c, lady in 12d's armrest), R23 ('is that chandelier going to keep getting bigger'), R41 ('light fixtures are protected'), R26 all pair card_pct 0.754-0.996 with dense_pct 0.025-0.201. Specificity and concrete detail are easy things for an explicit criterion to reward, and these captions are maximally specific; but their specificity is spent re-describing rather than extending.

proposals.name: Avoids off-the-shelf joke templates
proposals.instruction: Score freedom from prefabricated comic frames. 10 = the line's shape is not a recognizable stock structure. 0 = it is poured into a familiar mold: 'you think that's bad, [worse thing]', '[thing] is fine, but it isn't [pun]', a symmetrical two-item comparison whose second item is the punch, or a 'this X is on me if you never Y' bargain joke. Score structure only; a template can be filled with fresh content and still score 0 here.
proposals.rationale: R59 ('you think that's bad, my husband is an o.b.g.y.n') has the slice's lowest dense_pct, 0.004, at card_pct 0.896; R55 ('student of the year is fine, son, but it isn't best in show') and R37 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') and R24 sit at card_pct 0.922-0.958 with dense_pct 0.097-0.133. A bank checking for a clean setup and a clear payoff will score a well-executed template highly, since template captions are by construction well-formed.

proposals.name: Institutional vocabulary reframes the stakes rather than supplying a pun
proposals.instruction: Composite. First ask whether the line imports vocabulary from an institution — leases, billing, HR, litigation, parenting, medicine. If it does not, score 5. If it does: 10 = the vocabulary recasts what the scene is about, importing a whole system of obligations the picture did not have; 0 = the vocabulary is present only because one of its words literally matches something drawn, i.e. it is A03 wearing a suit.
proposals.rationale: The same lexical field falls on both sides of the disagreement, so the discriminating property is the use, not the field. Reframing: R15 ('if this doesn't break our lease'), R57 ('getting rid of the lawyer is going to cost you'), R35, at dense_pct 0.901-0.994 and card_pct 0.157-0.272. Punning: R53 ('selected for downsizing'), R54 ('hidden fees from thin air'), R20 ('phil from liquidations'), at card_pct 0.804-0.926 and dense_pct 0.084-0.165. A criterion that merely detects 'domain-specific language' credits both.

proposals.name: Names a real interior state a person actually has
proposals.instruction: Score the presence of recognizable human interiority. 10 = the line reports a genuine feeling — resignation, small regret, petty pride, exhausted patience, wounded self-justification — that a reader recognizes from their own life, stated without sentiment. 5 = an attitude is implied but generic. 0 = no interiority at all; the speaker is a delivery mechanism for a gag and has no discernible inner state.
proposals.rationale: R21 ('this is so much easier. i wish i thought of it sooner'), R15 ('i don't have any better ideas'), R51 ('simpler than deciding what to bring, but definitely more work'), R45 ('try not to overthink it') run dense_pct 0.887-0.994 with card_pct 0.117-0.272. These captions contain no wordplay, no reference, and no visible structure — nothing an explicit bank is likely to be scoring — yet they are among the dense model's very top items.

proposals.name: Key referent withheld; deixis points off the page
proposals.instruction: Score how much the sentence leans on unresolved pointing words. 10 = the central noun is never named — 'it', 'this one', 'either', 'anything', 'him' — and the reader must fetch the referent from outside the text. 5 = one unresolved pointer among named nouns. 0 = every referent is explicitly named inside the caption.
proposals.rationale: R60 ('i think i'll mount this one on the ceiling'), R19 ('what if i don't identify with either'), R09 ('unplugging it'), R50 ('it's only until we board the plane') span dense_pct 0.769-0.966 at card_pct 0.079-0.232. Unresolved deixis is the concrete lexical signature of a caption that hands work to the reader; explicit criteria typically treat vagueness as a defect, which would actively push these down.

proposals.name: Passes the overheard test as real human speech
proposals.instruction: Score whether a person could plausibly say this sentence aloud in the moment it depicts. 10 = natural cadence, contractions, run-ons, correction mid-sentence, the rhythm of actual talk. 5 = stilted but sayable. 0 = the syntax is contorted to reach a punchline or to seed a pun — an essayistic, literary, or over-nested construction nobody speaks.
proposals.rationale: Written-not-spoken lines cluster on the scorecard-high side: R38 ('so litigation continues to exist in advanced civilizations'), R32 ('think of a delay between one and ten hours'), R05 ('you flit home reeking of pollen and nectar'), card_pct 0.797-0.928 at dense_pct 0.059-0.182. Spoken-sounding lines cluster on the dense-high side: R02, R30, R17. Fluency and grammaticality criteria would reward the literary constructions; a naturalness criterion separates them.

proposals.name: Flat delivery paired with dark or high-stakes content
proposals.instruction: Composite. Rate the darkness or magnitude of what the line implies (mortality, humiliation, a life-altering disclosure, extinction, being trapped), then rate the escalation in its delivery. 10 = maximum implication delivered with zero escalation — grave content in an unbothered voice. 5 = mild stakes, mild delivery, or heavy stakes with matching heaviness. 0 = the stakes are shouted, or the content is milked as a punchline beat rather than dropped as an aside.
proposals.rationale: R22 ('i'll be waiting for a princess... not a prince'), R12 ('i don't see any signs of intelligent life anywhere'), R56 ('that's because i am talking in a tin can'), R31 ('the best part is ... no fox news') carry dense_pct 0.719-0.949 at card_pct 0.016-0.219 — heavy implications thrown away casually. The dense-low comparison is R37 and R28, dark material that is instead staged for the laugh (card_pct 0.918-0.980, dense_pct 0.021-0.133). Neither darkness alone nor flatness alone separates them; the interaction does.

proposals.name: Caption length and clause count
proposals.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of textual bulk: count words and independent/subordinate clauses. 0 = a bare fragment or single short clause of roughly five words or fewer; 5 = one full sentence of moderate length, roughly ten to fifteen words; 10 = thirty or more words, or three or more chained clauses, or two or more sentences. Judge extent only. Do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the caption is funny, whether it is too wordy, or whether brevity helps it. A long caption and a short caption can both score correctly here; you are measuring quantity of text, nothing else.
proposals.rationale: Sheer word count is a length proxy that any text model can latch onto independently of comic merit, and it varies enormously across this slice: R50 runs roughly thirty words with two embedded relative clauses and R43 chains a concessive plus a conditional across two clauses, while R11 ('did we forget anything') and R51 ('and now we wait') are four-word fragments. R28 is likewise a four-word fragment. Length also plausibly affects reception for non-quality reasons on the receiving side (scan speed, layout fit under a drawing), so it is predictive without being the thing we want to credit. Declaring it a nuisance prevents the bank from importing a verbosity dial.

proposals.name: Explicit lexical naming of the depicted object or setting
proposals.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption explicitly names, in words, a concrete physical object, fixture, animal, room, or vehicle that is evidently the thing being drawn, rather than referring to it only by a pronoun or leaving it unnamed. 0 = no concrete depicted object is named at all; the caption uses only pronouns, deixis ('this', 'it', 'him') or abstractions. 5 = one concrete object is named once in passing. 10 = the depicted object is named explicitly and is also the grammatical focus, or is named more than once, or is named together with its setting. Count nouns only, and count them whether or not they are used punningly. Judge extent of naming only. Do NOT judge whether naming the object is a good or bad move, whether it spoils or sharpens the joke, or whether the caption is funny.
proposals.rationale: Repeat entrants learn the house habit of letting the drawing carry the referent and writing pure in-world dialogue; first-time submitters more often lexicalize what is already visible. That difference in entrant experience leaves an exact textual fingerprint: R07 and R46 both name 'chandelier' outright, R41 names 'light fixtures', R40 names 'fixture', R32 names the 'circus breaker'. Against these, R11, R28, R51 and R56 name nothing depicted at all and lean entirely on pronouns and deixis. Entrant experience is a plausibly real driver of reception that is not itself caption quality (a veteran's habit can be scored as fluency), but the same experience plausibly does also produce genuinely better jokes, so this is tagged mixed rather than pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: submitter's familiarity with the contest's conventions (novice one-off entrant vs. repeat veteran entrant)

proposals.name: Dated news-cycle and pandemic-era vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption contains vocabulary that anchors it to a specific short-lived news period: epidemiological or public-health terms of art, named relief or benefit programs, references to cancelled or postponed gatherings, sanitizing and disinfection routines, vaccination controversy vocabulary. 0 = the caption is period-neutral and could have been written in any decade. 5 = one such term appears but is incidental. 10 = such vocabulary is the caption's central premise and the caption would be unintelligible outside that period. Judge extent of period anchoring only. Do NOT judge whether topicality is fresh, stale, clever, or tasteless, and do NOT judge whether the caption is funny.
proposals.rationale: Which week a submitter happened to enter is entirely outside the text, but it stamps the text hard, and it can shift reception (a whole cohort of same-week entries competes against and resembles each other) without any of that being caption quality. The fingerprint is unmistakable in this slice: R01 uses 'herd immunity', R04 names 'his full 1200 stimulus', R24 says 'anti-vacs', R37 has 'run it through the dishwasher to sanitize it', and R17 has 'we're not cancelling rehearsal again'. Period stamping is a nuisance in the strict sense: the calendar week does not make a caption better or worse, so mixed is false. Judges should be able to score this fingerprint without knowing anything about the round.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing — which calendar week's contest round the caption was written for

proposals.name: Named partisan political figures and outlets
proposals.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption names, or unmistakably designates, a real partisan political figure, party, campaign, or news outlet. 0 = no political person, party, campaign or outlet is referenced. 5 = one such reference appears as a passing modifier. 10 = a named political figure or outlet is the caption's subject, or two or more such references appear. Judge extent of political reference only. Do NOT judge whether the reference is accurate, fair, agreeable, well-aimed, or funny, and do NOT let your own view of the figure or outlet move the score in either direction.
proposals.rationale: Writing to a venue's presumed political sympathies is a social effect on reception that lives upstream of the text and is not comic craft, but it leaves an obvious lexical trace. In this slice R15 names 'marjorie taylor greene', R30 names 'the trump lure', R42 says 'if trump wins again', and R49 says 'no fox news'. All four are legible as partisan-audience alignment independent of whether the joke lands. Because shared politics can win favour from a like-minded reader for reasons that have nothing to do with the caption being a good contest entry, and because the political community a submitter belongs to is not plausibly a cause of genuine comic quality, this is tagged as a pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the submitter's political community and the assumed politics of the venue's readership

proposals.name: Workplace and professional jargon register
proposals.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption is written in the vocabulary of a workplace or credentialed profession: human-resources, corporate-finance, legal, medical, banking, or administrative terms of art, job titles, department names, and institutional processes. 0 = wholly everyday domestic or conversational vocabulary. 5 = one workplace or professional term appears. 10 = the caption is built out of such vocabulary, or names a department, credential, or formal institutional process. Judge extent of register only. Do NOT judge whether the jargon is used correctly, whether it is apt for the scene, or whether the caption is funny.
proposals.rationale: What a submitter does for a living is unobservable, but it stains their word choice, and the resulting register can be rewarded because it flatters a professional-class readership rather than because the joke is good. The trace is dense here: R19 'selected for downsizing', R34 'phil from liquidations', R23 'getting rid of the lawyer is going to cost you', R12 'litigation continues to exist in advanced civilizations', R08 'hidden fees', R26 'you student loan people', R13 'o.b.g.y.n'. Compare R56 and R51, which carry no occupational vocabulary at all. Tagged mixed because a submitter who works in a domain may also genuinely observe sharper things about it, so discounting this channel should be reported as a sensitivity band rather than a flat correction.
proposals.upstream_parent: submitter's occupation and professional milieu (and the venue readership's occupational skew)

proposals.name: Orthographic and typographic care
proposals.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of departures from standard written orthography: missing or misplaced apostrophes, misspelled words, nonstandard abbreviation or punctuation of acronyms, unpunctuated or oddly spaced numerals and times, missing sentence punctuation where a sentence boundary clearly falls, and inconsistent spacing. 0 = fully standard orthography throughout. 5 = one clear departure. 10 = three or more departures, or one departure that renders a word nonstandard enough to require re-reading. Ignore uniform lowercasing and ignore the absence of terminal question marks, since those are corpus-wide artefacts and not submitter behaviour. Judge extent of departure only. Do NOT judge whether the errors are charming, sloppy, or deliberate, and do NOT judge whether the caption is funny.
proposals.rationale: Whether anyone reread or copy-edited a submission is invisible, but it leaves a clean orthographic fingerprint, and copy cleanliness can move a reader's impression for reasons wholly separate from comic merit. In this slice R36 writes 'its hard to decide' with the apostrophe dropped, R24 writes 'anti-vacs' for anti-vax, R43 renders the time as '11 30' with no colon, and R13 punctuates the credential as 'o.b.g.y.n'. Against these, R21 and R44 are apostrophe-correct and internally consistent. Tagged mixed honestly: care taken over a submission plausibly correlates with care taken over the joke itself, so the discount must be reported alongside the undiscounted readout.
proposals.upstream_parent: proofreading effort and editorial assistance available before submission

proposals.name: Overt homophone and sound-alike substitution machinery
proposals.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption contains a visible word-substitution device: a word swapped for a near-homophone, a compound respelled, a fixed idiom with one member replaced, or a term deployed simultaneously in a literal and a figurative sense. 0 = no substitution device is present; the wording is straightforwardly literal. 5 = one such device appears once. 10 = the caption's whole structure is the device, or more than one device is stacked. Judge presence and extent of the mechanism only. Do NOT judge whether the wordplay lands, whether it is groanworthy or elegant, whether it is original, or whether the caption is funny.
proposals.rationale: The presence of pun machinery is a countable form feature that a text model can detect from orthography alone, and it is separable from whether the pun succeeds. The slice separates cleanly on it: R32 swaps 'circuit' for 'circus breaker', R52 swaps holidays for 'hollandaise', R36 puns on 'the poles', R40 turns 'fixture' literal, and R48 literalizes 'the elephant in the room'. Meanwhile R58, R29 and R11 carry no substitution device whatsoever. Because pun-presence is a template a scorer can reward mechanically regardless of execution, it must be declared a nuisance and kept out of the bank rather than promoted as a criterion.

proposals.name: Front-loaded interjections, discourse markers, and emphatic punctuation
proposals.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption opens with, or is punctuated by, conversational scaffolding rather than beginning directly on content: sentence-initial discourse markers and interjections ('well', 'so', 'okay', 'yeah', 'wow', 'watch out', 'and'), tag words, and emphatic punctuation such as exclamation marks and ellipses. 0 = the caption begins directly on its content with no marker and uses no emphatic punctuation. 5 = one opening marker or one emphatic mark. 10 = an opening marker plus additional interjections or emphatic punctuation elsewhere in the line. Judge extent of scaffolding only. Do NOT judge whether the scaffolding sounds natural, whether it earns its space, or whether the caption is funny.
proposals.rationale: Opening filler and emphatic marks are pure orthographic habit and are trivially countable, yet they change how conversational and how 'spoken' a line reads, which can shift reception on grounds unrelated to comic merit. The slice varies widely: R01 opens 'watch out!' with an exclamation, R46 opens 'just my luck!', R26 opens 'wow,', R10 opens 'well, there's your problem', R14 opens 'yeah', R44 and R38 both open on 'okay', and R49 uses a spaced ellipsis. By contrast R18, R29 and R60 open directly on content with no marker and no emphatic punctuation. Nothing about this feature is comic craft, so it is a pure nuisance.

proposals.name: Numeric and deictic specificity
proposals.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption contains concrete numbers or precise coordinates: digits, spelled-out quantities, sums of money, weights, durations, clock times, seat or row designations, counts, and dates. 0 = no numeric or precisely enumerated content of any kind. 5 = one number or quantity appears. 10 = two or more distinct numeric specifications appear, or a number carries the caption's premise. Judge extent of numeric content only. Do NOT judge whether the numbers are plausible, well chosen, or comically precise, and do NOT judge whether the caption is funny.
proposals.rationale: Digit and quantity density is a countable orthographic feature, and 'specificity' is a well-known thing scorers reward as a proxy for vividness even when it does no comic work. The slice spans the full range: R50 specifies seats '13c' and '12d', R04 specifies 'his full 1200 stimulus', R25 specifies '45 pounds', R43 specifies '11 30', R05 specifies 'between one and ten hours', R58 specifies 'about three years', and R38 counts 'on three'. Against these, R51, R29 and R57 contain no numeric content at all. Since a number can be inserted into any caption without improving it, this must be a declared nuisance.

proposals.name: Kinship framing and first-name familiar address
proposals.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption is framed around household or family relationships, or addresses its listener by a personal first name or familiar role term. Count kinship nouns ('mom', 'dad', 'daddy', 'son', 'husband', 'wife'), possessive family references, domestic-curfew or spousal-complaint framing, and first-name vocatives. 0 = no kinship term, no family framing, and no personal name of address. 5 = one kinship term or one first-name vocative. 10 = the caption's whole premise is a family relationship, or it combines a kinship term with a name of address. Judge extent of kinship and familiar-address framing only. Do NOT judge whether the family framing is warm, tired, relatable, or well observed, and do NOT judge whether the caption is funny.
proposals.rationale: A submitter's own household is invisible to the model, but it drives which relationship they reach for when inventing a speaker, and it leaves a hard lexical fingerprint. This slice is full of it: R04 says 'daddy', R13 says 'my husband', R25 says 'my mom ... my dad', R55 addresses a 'son', R39 and R43 are both spousal-curfew complaints, and R41, R53 and R34 use the first names 'don', 'ronny' and 'phil'. Compare R12, R22 and R59, which have no kinship or naming content at all. Life-stage cohort can align a caption with a similarly aged readership for reasons that are demographic rather than comic, and cohort itself is not plausibly a cause of genuine caption quality, so this is a pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: submitter's life stage and household composition (age cohort, parenthood, marital status)

proposals.name: Deadpan delivery of high-stakes or absurd content
proposals.instruction: Score how flatly and matter-of-factly the caption states something emotionally loaded, alarming, or absurd, with no exclamatory or emotional markers. 10 = the caption states something startling or extreme in completely plain, unemotional language, as if it were routine. 0 = the caption's emotional register matches its content exactly (calm content stated calmly, or shocking content stated with visible alarm/emphasis), so there is no incongruity between tone and content.
proposals.rationale: R01, R05, R22, R28, R50, and R60 are all flat, understated lines that dense ranks very high; contrast R07 ("wow, you student loan people really know how to track someone down") and R09 ("just my luck!..."), whose exclamatory framing the scorecard rewards instead. Dense may be crediting the comic value of flat delivery that the scorecard's fixed criteria don't have a slot for.

proposals.name: Obliqueness of reference to the depicted subject
proposals.instruction: Score how indirectly the caption refers to the cartoon's central object or subject. 10 = the subject is never named; it is referred to only via pronoun ("it", "this", "that one") or left fully implicit. 0 = the caption explicitly names or labels the subject/theme word outright.
proposals.rationale: R41 ("mount this one on the ceiling") and R47 ("unplugging it") never name their subject and sit in dense_high_card_low, while R02, R09, and R58 all explicitly say "chandelier" and sit in dense_low_card_high. The scorecard may reward explicit naming as evidence of being on-topic, which dense does not require.

proposals.name: Joke resolves within the line vs. requires outside inference
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption's comedic logic is fully explained by the words on the page, versus requiring the reader to supply unstated context to get the joke. 10 = a reader with zero access to the (unseen) cartoon can reconstruct the entire joke mechanism from the text alone. 0 = the line is only a fragment or reaction whose humor depends entirely on a scene or backstory the text never states.
proposals.rationale: R51 ("...has now turned on the 'applause' sign") and R13 (the whole threat and consequence are spelled out) are fully self-sufficient and sit in dense_low_card_high, while R22 ("and now we wait") and R60 ("try not to overthink it"), both dense_high_card_low, supply almost no internal context. The scorecard may reward self-contained legibility that a text-only judge can score with confidence.

proposals.name: Density of identifiable wordplay/puns
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the caption's humor is built on one or more clearly spottable puns or double meanings. 10 = the line's core joke is a clean, easily identified pun or double meaning. 0 = no wordplay of any kind is present.
proposals.rationale: R09 ("chandelier season"), R52 ("circus breaker"), R40 ("hollandaise"), and R37 ("ballplayers") are all pun-built and land in dense_low_card_high, while R01, R22, and R43, all dense_high_card_low, contain no wordplay at all. This suggests the scorecard over-credits recognizable pun mechanics relative to the dense model.

proposals.name: Dependence on a named real-world topical/political reference
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption's humor depends on a specific, dateable real-world person, policy, or news event named in the text. 10 = the joke requires recognizing a named current person, policy, or event to land. 0 = the caption is entirely evergreen, with nothing tying it to a specific moment in time.
proposals.rationale: R45 ("if trump wins again"), R46 ("marjorie taylor greene"), R48 ("trump lure"), and R17 ("herd immunity") all lean on topical/political reference and sit in dense_low_card_high, while the dense_high_card_low set (e.g., R01, R22, R41) is almost entirely evergreen. The scorecard may over-credit topicality that the dense model discounts.

proposals.name: Implied social/status expectation reversed within the line
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption sets up a familiar social or status expectation and then inverts or subverts it within the same line. 10 = a clear expectation about power, hierarchy, or social role is established and then flipped. 0 = no such setup-and-reversal is present; the line is a straightforward statement.
proposals.rationale: R24 ("do you have any idea who you're talking to") and R55 ("ignore him. you now report directly to me") both hinge on a sudden status inversion and are both dense_high_card_low. The scorecard's fixed criteria may not have a slot for this kind of pragmatic reversal.

proposals.name: Vividness of the scenario conjured by the text alone
proposals.instruction: Score how specific and concrete a mental scene the caption conjures, independent of the actual cartoon. 10 = a reader can picture a detailed, specific situation just from the words. 0 = the line is so generic or abstract that no particular scenario comes to mind.
proposals.rationale: R01 ("at least i know i'm a puppet") and R44 ("switch from the bass to the viola"), both dense_high_card_low, conjure sharp, specific scenes, while R11 ("chicken or rabbit"), dense_low_card_high, stays vague. Dense may reward this vividness more than the scorecard does.

proposals.name: Absence of filler/hedge words around the punchline
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the caption is load-bearing for the joke versus filler. 10 = every word contributes to the joke; no throat-clearing exclamations or hedges ("wow", "well", "okay", "just my luck") precede the payoff. 0 = the caption opens with or contains clear filler/hedge language that could be deleted with no loss of meaning.
proposals.rationale: R09 ("just my luck! chandelier season...") and R26 ("okay on three yank...") both open with filler and sit in dense_low_card_high, while R43 ("did we forget anything") and R50 ("did i miss anything"), both dense_high_card_low, are pure economy with zero filler.

proposals.name: Pun spelled out vs. left compressed for the reader to complete
proposals.instruction: Score whether a pun's second meaning is made explicit by surrounding words, versus compressed into a single word/phrase the reader must decode unaided. 10 = the sentence structure explicitly walks the reader to the pun's alternate meaning (e.g., parallel phrasing that names both senses). 0 = the pun is a single compressed word/phrase with no scaffolding, and the reader must supply the second meaning entirely on their own.
proposals.rationale: R09 ("chandelier season doesn't begin until next week" — the "season" phrasing spells out the hunting pun) and R40 ("depressed around the hollandaise" — phrased to walk the reader to "holidays") are both dense_low_card_high and fully scaffolded, while R56 ("i don't trust the poles anymore"), dense_high_card_low, leaves the poles/polls pun fully compressed with no scaffolding.

proposals.name: Internal two-clause setup-then-payoff structure
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption itself contains two distinct clauses — an internal setup (a condition, scenario, or claim) followed by a distinct payoff/consequence clause — versus being a single flat clause. 10 = a clear two-part "if/but/and-then" structure with a setup clause and a distinct payoff clause. 0 = a single, unbroken clause with no internal setup-payoff split.
proposals.rationale: R13 ("go and enjoy the lights if you must, but if you are not back by 11 30 you're sleeping on the screen door again") and R34 ("i don't care, we're not cancelling rehearsal again. two three four") both show clear internal structure and sit in dense_low_card_high, while R22 ("and now we wait") and R43 ("did we forget anything"), both dense_high_card_low, are single flat clauses.

proposals.name: Specific persona markers (named addressee or verbal tic)
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the caption signals a particular speaker's distinct voice via a named addressee, in-group term, or idiosyncratic phrasing. 10 = the line names a specific addressee or contains a clearly idiosyncratic verbal habit that only this character would use. 0 = the line is voice-neutral and could be said by anyone in any context.
proposals.rationale: R33 ("we're dinosaurs, ronny... we don't do whimsy") and R38 ("that's phil from liquidations") both name a specific person and sit in dense_low_card_high, while R22 ("and now we wait") and R60 ("try not to overthink it"), both dense_high_card_low, are voice-neutral, generic lines.

proposals.name: Caption reads as answer within an implied Q&A exchange
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption reads as a direct response to a specific, inferable unheard question, versus a standalone assertion. 10 = the line clearly completes a conversational exchange and the shape of the preceding question is easy to infer. 0 = the line is a self-contained assertion with no implied preceding question.
proposals.rationale: R28 ("about three years. how long have you been here") echoes back an implied question directly, and R05 ("no idea, let's just take the stairs") implies a preceding "what happened to the elevator" — both dense_high_card_low — while R33 ("we're dinosaurs, ronny... we don't do whimsy"), dense_low_card_high, is a flat declarative with no implied question.

proposals.name: Explicit self-correction / garden-path negation
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption sets up one reading and then explicitly negates or corrects it within the same line (e.g., "...not X", "not really X, more Y"). 10 = a clear self-correction/negation marker redirects the line's meaning partway through. 0 = the line proceeds straight through with no internal correction or negation of its own setup.
proposals.rationale: R08 ("i'll be waiting for a princess... not a prince") is a textbook garden-path correction and sits in dense_high_card_low, alongside R31 ("to begin with, i am not anti-vacs"), which opens by pre-empting an assumption — contrast R04 or R06, both dense_low_card_high, which state their content in one direction with no internal correction.

proposals.name: Institutional/bureaucratic register applied to an incongruous context
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption borrows recognizable formal, corporate, legal, or bureaucratic phrasing and applies it somewhere that register doesn't normally belong. 10 = the line clearly uses institutional/jargon phrasing (e.g., an HR euphemism, legal phrasing, competition terminology) in an absurd or mismatched context. 0 = the caption uses plain, everyday language throughout with no institutional register.
proposals.rationale: R06 ("you've been selected for downsizing, too") and R25 ("so litigation continues to exist in advanced civilizations") both apply institutional language to odd contexts and sit in dense_low_card_high; contrast the plain register of R01 ("at least i know i'm a puppet"), dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Morbid/dark content (death, injury, loss) as the comic engine
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption's humor is built directly on death, physical injury, loss, or decline. 10 = the central joke turns on dark subject matter (death, injury, loss) stated as the punchline's core content. 0 = the caption's content is entirely benign, with nothing dark or morbid.
proposals.rationale: R04 ("my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg") and R10 ("don't cry, now daddy can get his full 1200 stimulus", implying a death) both anchor their humor in dark content and sit in dense_low_card_high; R29 ("this fish is dead"), dense_high_card_low, shows the same device appearing on the other side too, so isolating darkness as its own axis lets a judge credit content-darkness independent of the flat delivery captured in A01.

proposals.name: Caption length / verbosity (word count, clause count)
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how long and multi-clause this caption is, purely as a word-count/structure measure (0 = extremely terse, roughly <=6 words with a single clause; 10 = long, multi-clause with an explicit setup plus payoff). Do not judge whether the length helps or hurts the joke -- score only how much text/structure is present.
proposals.rationale: dense_high_card_low items cluster around very short one-liners (R18 'did we forget anything'; R22 'and now we wait'), while dense_low_card_high items cluster around longer, multi-clause captions (R03 'she's a real beaut, don, but you'll have to throw it back...'; R37's airplane/emergency-exit bit). Length itself, not joke content, tracks the split.

proposals.name: Two-clause 'X, but Y' contrastive template
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much this caption follows an explicit two-part 'X, but Y' / 'X, however Y' contrastive template -- a clause establishing one expectation immediately reversed by a second clause joined with 'but'/'however'/similar. 0 = no such contrastive-conjunction structure; 10 = the entire caption is built as an explicit two-clause contrast. Do not judge whether the contrast is funny -- score only whether the template is present.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('...but you'll have to throw it back') and R12 ('the parts are cheap, but getting rid of the lawyer is going to cost you') both use the identical 'but'-contrast template despite falling on opposite sides of the disagreement (R03 dense_low_card_high, R12 dense_high_card_low), suggesting the template itself is doing independent work rather than tracking joke quality.

proposals.name: Direct named/titled address (vocative)
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the caption directly addresses a named or titled individual (a vocative like a first name, 'sir', 'ma'am', pet name, or role-title used to address the listener within the caption). 0 = no addressee named; 10 = caption opens or is built around directly naming/addressing someone. Do not judge whether naming someone makes the caption better -- score only the presence of a direct address.
proposals.rationale: R03 addresses 'don' directly ('she's a real beaut, don...') and R42 addresses 'ronny' directly ('we're dinosaurs, ronny...'); both are card-favored items (dense_low_card_high), suggesting named address may be a card-favored surface cue unrelated to joke construction.

proposals.name: Political/current-events proper-noun density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the caption explicitly names a real-world political figure, party, news event, or current-events keyword (e.g. a politician's name, 'stimulus', 'fox news', 'anti-vax', 'herd immunity', election language). 0 = no such reference; 10 = the caption's entire content is a direct real-world political/news reference. Do not judge whether the political reference is clever -- score only its presence/density.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('if trump wins again') and R54 ('no fox news') both invoke real-world politics/news directly; such references appear on both sides of the split (R01, R15, R31, R47 dense_low_card_high vs R54, R29 dense_high_card_low), indicating topicality is doing independent work in at least one model's scoring rather than reflecting joke craft.

proposals.name: Discourse-marker hedge opener (veteran stylistic tic)
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the caption opens with a short discourse-marker or hedge phrase (e.g. 'well,', 'okay,', 'no idea,', 'at least,', 'ladies and gentlemen,') before its main statement. 0 = caption launches directly into its main statement with no such opener; 10 = caption is built entirely around a prominent framing opener. Do not judge whether the opener is skillfully used -- score only its presence.
proposals.rationale: Repeat entrants to a recurring contest often develop recognizable stock framing devices; R07 opens with 'ladies and gentlemen,' and R17 opens with 'no idea,' -- these openers recur across items on both sides of the split (R07 dense_low_card_high; R17 dense_high_card_low), consistent with a submitter-style tic that a familiar community could reward independent of the specific joke's merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's contest experience / seniority in the submitter community

proposals.name: Continuity/repetition cue words ('again', 'still', 'every time')
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the caption uses continuity/repetition language (words like 'again', 'still', 'once again', 'every time', 'now again') to frame the depicted moment as one instance of a recurring pattern or ongoing relationship. 0 = no such continuity cue; 10 = the caption's core content is built around a 'this keeps happening' framing. Do not judge whether the recurring-saga framing is funny -- score only its presence.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('once again you flit home') and R35 ('keep getting bigger every time you tell this story') both use continuity cues implying a recurring domestic saga between the depicted characters, and both are dense_low_card_high; a crowd's engagement with an implied backstory is a social/narrative effect distinct from a single caption's construction quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: process dynamics on the receiving side (crowd favors implied ongoing-relationship narratives)

proposals.name: Specialized professional/technical vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the caption uses specialized professional, technical, medical, legal, or scientific vocabulary/jargon (field-specific abbreviations or terms a general audience would not use casually). 0 = plain everyday vocabulary only; 10 = caption is built around specialized/technical terminology. Do not judge whether the jargon makes the joke better -- score only its presence.
proposals.rationale: R33 uses the medical abbreviation 'o.b.g.y.n' and R49 uses the legal/civic term 'litigation'; such terms plausibly reflect the author's specific professional background supplying ready vocabulary, which can read as clever through unfamiliarity/specificity independent of actual joke craft.

proposals.name: Genericity -- caption transportable to any cartoon
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how generic/portable the caption is -- i.e. how easily it could be dropped unchanged into a different, unrelated cartoon without needing any edits (0 = tightly tied to specific concrete details that could only belong to one particular scene; 10 = fully generic, no scene-specific detail at all). Do not judge whether genericity makes the caption funnier or weaker -- score only how context-independent the wording is.
proposals.rationale: R18 ('did we forget anything') and R22 ('and now we wait') are highly generic lines with no scene-specific nouns at all and both fall in dense_high_card_low along with R09 and R56 of the same type; a prolific entrant with time/resources to submit many entries per contest may favor such reusable one-liners as a numbers-game strategy rather than crafting a scene-specific joke.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's submission strategy / volume (prolific submitters reuse portable stock lines)

proposals.name: Precise numeric/quantitative detail
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the caption includes a precise numeric or quantitative detail (a specific dollar amount, a specific time, a specific count/measurement -- not a vague quantity like 'some' or 'a lot'). 0 = no numeric/quantitative detail; 10 = the caption's key content is built around a precise number. Do not judge whether the precision improves the joke -- score only its presence.
proposals.rationale: R19 ('full 1200 stimulus') and R32 ('not back by 11 30') both embed precise numeric details and are both dense_low_card_high; extra drafting/polish invested by an author or editor can accrete such concrete numeric specificity as a mark of craft investment distinct from whether the underlying joke concept itself is funny.

proposals.name: Ellipsis/dash comedic-pause punctuation
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the caption uses an ellipsis ('...') or em/en-dash to mark a deliberate pause before a final twist word/phrase. 0 = no such punctuation-marked pause; 10 = the caption's punchline is explicitly set off by an ellipsis/dash pause. Do not judge whether the pause timing is effective -- score only whether the punctuation device is present.
proposals.rationale: R34 ('i'll be waiting for a princess... not a prince') and R42 ('we're dinosaurs, ronny... we don't do whimsy') both use an ellipsis to stage a pause before a twist; the two rows fall on opposite sides of the split (R34 dense_high_card_low, R42 dense_low_card_high), showing the typographic habit is not itself locked to one model's construct and can function as an independent formatting fingerprint.

proposals.name: Conversational naturalness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line sounds effortless and plausibly spoken by a real person; score 0 when it sounds stilted, artificial, or linguistically unnatural.
proposals.rationale: R01, R02, R07, and R29 use ordinary conversational phrasing that carries humor without elaborate construction.

proposals.name: Comedic compression
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption creates a complete comic situation with very few words; score 0 when it is padded, repetitive, or requires excess setup.
proposals.rationale: R02, R07, R09, and R43 achieve their effect through extremely economical wording.

proposals.name: Productive ambiguity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line leaves an intriguing gap that invites a specific comic inference while remaining understandable; score 0 when it is either fully obvious or merely unclear.
proposals.rationale: R02, R07, R09, and R29 withhold just enough information to make the reader mentally complete the situation.

proposals.name: Deadpan understatement
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an absurd or consequential situation is delivered with calm, matter-of-fact restraint; score 0 when the caption announces, exaggerates, or explains its own humor.
proposals.rationale: R06, R11, R45, and R50 frame unusual circumstances in notably restrained language.

proposals.name: Practical-stakes escalation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary practical concern unexpectedly expands into a much larger personal or logistical consequence; score 0 when the stakes remain flat or unrelated.
proposals.rationale: R06 turns a repair idea into a lease concern, while R15 turns cheap parts into an expensive legal problem; R45 similarly contrasts simplicity with greater work.

proposals.name: Fresh language reinterpretation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar phrase, cliché, or technical expression is reinterpreted in a surprising but coherent context; score 0 when wording is literal, predictable, or disconnected.
proposals.rationale: R01 recontextualizes troubleshooting language, R34 literalizes “tin can” communication, and R47 gives “best part” an unexpected political meaning.

proposals.name: Concrete detail with comic leverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one or two precise details materially sharpen the comic premise or image; score 0 when details are generic, decorative, or absent.
proposals.rationale: R03 uses bass and viola, R35 uses an elephant and an elevator, and R39 specifies mounting something on the ceiling.

proposals.name: Topical-reference integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a public figure, trend, or current topic is essential to the joke’s mechanism; score 0 when it is merely name-dropped or could be removed without changing the line.
proposals.rationale: R14, R18, and R25 all use Trump-related references, but the criterion distinguishes meaningful transformation from detachable topical labeling.

proposals.name: Wordplay precision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the pun or verbal substitution is immediate, exact, and meaningfully connected to the premise; score 0 when it depends on a strained sound, misspelling, or weak semantic link.
proposals.rationale: R28 depends on “poles,” R31 on “anti-vacs,” and R30 on “depressed around the hollandaise,” illustrating varying degrees of verbal fit.

proposals.name: Status or role reversal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption sharply flips expected authority, identity, dependence, or social position; score 0 when all roles remain conventional and unchanged.
proposals.rationale: R16 reverses expected romantic roles, R37 makes self-awareness a puppet’s trait, and R58 abruptly transfers authority to the speaker.

proposals.name: Standalone intelligibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a reader can understand the situation and comic implication from the line alone; score 0 when it is an opaque fragment with insufficient textual cues.
proposals.rationale: R10, R13, and R54 provide minimal context and can feel incomplete without additional information, unlike more self-contained lines such as R06.

proposals.name: Syntactic readability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when grammar, punctuation, abbreviations, and clause structure are effortless to parse; score 0 when errors, awkward compression, or overloaded syntax impede reading.
proposals.rationale: R12 and R60 contain long, heavily nested constructions, while R26 uses an awkwardly punctuated abbreviation that can interrupt fluency.

proposals.name: Setup-payoff proportion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the setup supplies exactly enough information for a satisfying turn and the payoff arrives promptly; score 0 when explanation overwhelms the joke or no clear turn develops.
proposals.rationale: R12 and R60 devote substantial wording to setup before reaching their final image, making proportionality especially relevant.

proposals.name: Tactful handling of sensitive material
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when sensitive subjects are handled with layered comic insight rather than simple harm, shock, or humiliation; score 0 when the punchline relies almost entirely on distress, disability, illness, or cruelty.
proposals.rationale: R05, R26, and R46 use crying, reproductive health, weight, and disability as comic material, making the quality of treatment important beyond mere topical boldness.

proposals.name: Reference accessibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the humor remains clear to a broad reader without specialized, transient, or culturally narrow knowledge; score 0 when understanding depends almost entirely on such knowledge.
proposals.rationale: R14 and R18 rely on political familiarity, while R51 and R52 depend on more specific knowledge about ballplayers or insect behavior.

proposals.name: Question-format framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much is the caption phrased as a direct question or question-like exchange? Judge only the visible interrogative format, not whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: Question framing may track familiar dialogue conventions without measuring caption quality. Examples include R01, R04, R07, and R10.

proposals.name: Political-current-affairs markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain explicit political, public-policy, or current-affairs names and terms? Judge only their presence, not whether the reference is good.
proposals.rationale: Political vocabulary can attract attention or trigger shared associations independently of caption quality. Examples include R18, R25, R39, R45, and R52.

proposals.name: Institutional register
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use legal, financial, bureaucratic, corporate, or other institutional vocabulary? Judge only the register, not whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: Institutional language may correlate with audience familiarity or venue conventions without representing quality. Examples include R01, R05, R13, R40, R53, and R60.

proposals.name: Clause and detail load
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain multiple clauses, qualifiers, or concrete situational details? Judge only textual length and detail density, not whether they improve the caption.
proposals.rationale: Longer, information-dense submissions can behave differently because of presentation habits rather than quality. Examples include R11, R19, R21, and R41.

proposals.name: Imperative procedure language
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption instruct someone to act, follow steps, wait, operate something, or troubleshoot? Judge only the instructional form, not whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: Operational wording may resemble familiar workplace or troubleshooting templates without measuring quality. Examples include R12, R16, R22, R23, and R55.

proposals.name: Time-sensitive framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain dates, times, seasons, delays, temporary windows, or other explicitly time-bound cues? Judge only the temporal cues, not whether they are good.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing can make certain temporal references more salient, while timely framing may also genuinely help construction; therefore this is a sensitivity channel. Examples include R24, R41, R57, and R59.

proposals.name: Standardized copyediting
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the text show syntactically complete, grammatically normalized, and smoothly integrated sentence mechanics? Judge only visible normalization, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: Professional editing may leave a mechanical fingerprint and may also improve the underlying writing, so the channel is mixed. Examples include R06, R11, R19, and R34.

proposals.name: Personal insider referents
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption rely on named people, kinship roles, direct addressees, or presumed personal familiarity? Judge only the presence of these referents, not whether they are good.
proposals.rationale: A producer's network can supply recognizable names or insider relationships, while firsthand familiarity may also support genuinely better material. Examples include R02, R14, R46, R47, and R60.

proposals.name: Specialized scene markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain concrete role-specific mechanics, equipment, coordinates, procedures, or occupational setting details? Judge only the specificity of the scene, not whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: Access to specialized settings can leave textual traces and can also provide real subject knowledge, making this a mixed sensitivity channel. Examples include R21, R35, R50, R56, and R60.

proposals.name: Reusable template phrasing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use a familiar stock construction, catchphrase pattern, or reusable conversational template? Judge only formulaic resemblance, not whether the phrasing is good.
proposals.rationale: A receiving process may favor recognizable templates through familiarity effects even when that familiarity is unrelated to quality. Examples include R04, R23, R37, and R50.

proposals.name: Information-per-word
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when nearly every word establishes the situation or advances the comic turn; score 0 when the line is padded, repetitive, or too skeletal to form a usable premise.
proposals.rationale: R08, R39, and R53 convey substantial comic direction with very little wording, whereas R20 and R21 spend many words on details that may not proportionately sharpen the joke.

proposals.name: Deadpan restraint
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an absurd premise is delivered calmly without announcing the joke; score 0 when exclamations, emphatic commands, or explicit comic cues do the work.
proposals.rationale: R08, R15, and R42 use flat delivery, while R06 and R45 foreground their intended effect through urgent exclamations and instructions.

proposals.name: Semantic reframe
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary word or phrase naturally supports one reading and then snaps to another; score 0 when wording remains literal or produces a strained, unclear pun.
proposals.rationale: R09, R10, R29, and R60 exploit shifts in the meanings of familiar terms, unlike more literal lines such as R07 and R37.

proposals.name: Causal absurdity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the absurd consequence follows from a recognizable rule, procedure, or practical logic; score 0 when the weirdness has no inferable bridge from the premise.
proposals.rationale: R24, R48, and R51 derive their turns from recognizable cost, lease, and troubleshooting logic, while R22 and R37 offer less visible causal development.

proposals.name: Status reversal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line sharply flips who has authority, leverage, knowledge, or social standing; score 0 when the interpersonal relationship remains unchanged.
proposals.rationale: R04, R31, and R50 turn on altered authority or social standing, whereas R49 and R56 provide little relational movement.

proposals.name: Physical staging
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording creates an immediately pictureable action, object, or position that is essential to the joke; score 0 when it is abstract commentary with no stageable element.
proposals.rationale: R18, R26, and R57 supply concrete physical staging, while R14 and R25 remain comparatively abstract.

proposals.name: Earned detail
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when each concrete detail causes or intensifies the comic turn; score 0 when details are ornamental, exhaustive, or interchangeable.
proposals.rationale: The dishwasher detail in R47 and the elephant-elevator pairing in R57 materially drive their turns; the extensive seat and body-position description in R20 is more vulnerable to feeling decorative.

proposals.name: Productive omission
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line leaves a crucial fact unstated, inviting the reader to complete the scene while remaining interpretable; score 0 when it overexplains or is too incomplete to understand.
proposals.rationale: R08, R28, and R32 rely on the reader to supply missing context, while R13 and R20 spell out more of their situations.

proposals.name: Distinctive speaker voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when diction reveals a specific attitude or persona and would not fit many interchangeable speakers; score 0 when the wording sounds generic or anonymous.
proposals.rationale: R03, R46, and R47 have recognizable conversational attitudes, whereas R07, R25, and R37 could be spoken by almost anyone.

proposals.name: Cross-domain bridge
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when two distant domains are joined by one surprising but intelligible analogy or substitution; score 0 when the domains are merely juxtaposed or connected arbitrarily.
proposals.rationale: R03 links musical negotiation to social exchange, and R57 turns an idiom into an elevator scenario; R40 juxtaposes two losses with a less developed conceptual hinge.

proposals.name: Controlled escalation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary premise escalates to a larger consequence without abandoning the underlying situation; score 0 when the line adds an abrupt shock or unrelated pile-on.
proposals.rationale: R24 and R48 escalate practical problems while preserving their situations, whereas R40 and R43 move quickly to extreme consequences with less continuity.

proposals.name: Reference integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a named public or cultural reference changes the caption's mechanics or creates a second meaning; score 0 when the name is replaceable topical decoration.
proposals.rationale: R12 makes Fox News part of the conversational payoff, while the references in R22, R33, and R38 can function more like topical labels than structural components.

proposals.name: Register collision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal, professional, technical, or domestic language collides naturally with another register to create a precise mismatch; score 0 when jargon is decorative or the line stays in one register.
proposals.rationale: R24 combines legal and household-economic language, and R47 combines sanitation language with domestic troubleshooting; R14 and R43 lean more heavily on institutional vocabulary alone.

proposals.name: Turn-at-the-end
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the final clause or word is the precise point where the meaning, power, or image flips; score 0 when there is no timed reveal or the key idea arrives too early.
proposals.rationale: R05, R24, and R57 reserve their strongest reframe for the ending, while R01 and R07 announce their premises without a comparable terminal turn.

proposals.name: Conversational turn-taking
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line sounds like an apt response to an implied prior utterance, with natural rhythm and an unstated premise; score 0 when it reads like a label, slogan, or exposition no speaker would plausibly say.
proposals.rationale: R04, R41, and R46 sound like sharply situated replies, whereas R17, R37, and R56 read more like labels or bare fragments.

proposals.name: Boilerplate conversational framing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for the extent of stock conversational openings, closers, or filler formulas. Judge only the visible wording; do not judge whether it is good, funny, or contest-worthy.
proposals.rationale: Such formulas may predict familiarity and processing fluency without measuring caption quality. Examples include R08, R17, R24, and R52.

proposals.name: Numeric logistical specificity
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for the extent of numerals, times, measurements, counts, locations, or other logistical specifics. Count their presence only; do not judge whether the details improve the caption.
proposals.rationale: Data-like details can affect readability and memorability independently of entry quality. Examples include R14, R20, R33, and R43.

proposals.name: Orthographic informality
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for lowercase starts, omitted apostrophes, unconventional abbreviations, spelling variants, or irregular punctuation. Judge only the extent of these surface forms, not their correctness or quality.
proposals.rationale: Casual orthography can signal community style or alter processing without reflecting humor or craft. Examples include R15, R38, and R45.

proposals.name: Current-affairs anchoring
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for explicit references to politicians, public policies, government programs, or recognizable news controversies. Count topical references only; do not judge whether they are timely or effective.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: submission timing can determine whether such references are especially familiar. Textual fingerprint: named political and public-affairs references. Examples include R06, R28, R42, and R43. Timing may also help produce genuinely timely material, so this is mixed.

proposals.name: Broadcast performance register
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for announcer language, stage directions, magic-show cues, rehearsal count-ins, or other performance-script wording. Judge only the extent of this register, not whether the performance frame is amusing.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: a venue's house style or processing conventions may favor familiar performance formats. Textual fingerprint: broadcast and stage-performance phrasing. Examples include R13, R33, and R45.

proposals.name: Occupational institutional lexicon
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for visible terms associated with law, medicine, education, finance, corporate administration, or bureaucratic systems. Count domain vocabulary only; do not judge whether its use is insightful.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: an author's professional environment or network may supply specialized vocabulary. Textual fingerprint: occupational and institutional terms. Examples include R01, R12, R55, and R59. The same milieu may also provide domain knowledge that improves genuine work, so this is mixed.

proposals.name: Publication-like syntactic polish
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for surface markers such as complete sentences, conventional punctuation, balanced clauses, and smoothly integrated syntax. Judge only these visible markers; do not treat polish as evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: editing or drafting assistance can leave a polished textual trace that affects processing independently of underlying caption quality. Examples include R01, R20, and R33. Assistance may also improve the actual entry, so this is mixed.

proposals.name: Kinship household-role framing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for explicit kinship or household-role terms such as husband, son, mom, dad, spouse, or comparable family positions. Count role references only; do not judge whether the scenario is relatable.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: social milieu can shape which family-role situations are represented and recognized. Textual fingerprint: kinship and household-role vocabulary. Examples include R12, R19, and R27. Social experience may also contribute to genuine quality, so this is mixed.

proposals.name: Directive second-person voice
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for imperatives, commands, warnings, or direct second-person address. Count the interactional form only; do not judge whether the directive is clear or effective.
proposals.rationale: Directive language can alter reader engagement and processing without measuring the caption's quality. Examples include R25, R39, R54, and R60.

proposals.name: Fragmentary minimalism
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for sentence fragments, very short utterances, ellipses, or highly compressed syntax. Judge only the degree of compression; do not judge whether brevity is good or funny.
proposals.rationale: Very short forms may receive different processing from complete sentences while saying nothing about entry quality. Examples include R05, R08, R17, R24, and R50.
